problem.title: Two Sum
problem.summary: Find two numbers in an array that add up to a target

examples.source: if the array is 2, 7, 11, 15 and the target is 9, you'd return 0 and 1

requirements.text: Return indices of two different elements that sum to target
requirements.source: they have to be two different elements. Different indices.

history.text: Find two different elements that sum to target

requirements.source: You can assume there's exactly one valid answer

requirements.source: array can be up to about ten to the fourth elements

questions.text: Should I return the values or the indices of the two numbers?

questions.answer: Return the indices, not the values

questions.why: affects whether we need to handle multiple answers

questions.answer: Assume exactly one valid answer exists

questions.answer: No, must be two different elements/indices

estimate.rationale: classic easy, one pass with a hash map

plan.step: Create an empty hash map to store value -> index seen so far
Iterate through nums with index i and value num
plan.branch: or: sort + two pointers (loses original indices, needs extra bookkeeping)

plan.detail: check if complement already in seen

plan.step: If complement in seen, return [seen[complement], i]
Otherwise store seen[num] = i and continue

approaches.name: Brute force: check every pair
approaches.idea: Check every pair of indices to see if they sum to target.
approaches.why_not: At n=10,000 that's ~5·10⁷ pair checks — noticeably slower (tens to hundreds of ms, and scales quadratically) versus ~10,000 O(1) hash lookups for the optimal approach; also more code and nested loops to reason about.
approaches.tradeoffs: Simple and no extra memory, but too slow if n grows.
approaches.say_it: The naive approach is to check every pair of elements with nested loops, which is O(n²) and fine for tiny inputs but too slow at n=10,000.

approaches.name: Sort + two pointers
approaches.idea: Sort (value, original index) pairs, then use two pointers from both ends to find the target sum.
approaches.pseudocode:
pairs = sorted((v,i) for i,v in enumerate(nums))
lo,hi=0,n-1
while lo<hi:
  s=pairs[lo][0]+pairs[hi][0]
  if s==target: return indices
  elif s<target: lo+=1
  else: hi-=1
approaches.why_not: Requires an extra O(n) array of (value,index) pairs and an O(n log n) sort (~10,000·log2(10,000)≈130,000 comparisons) just to then do a linear scan — strictly more work and more code than one hash-map pass with O(n) time and simpler logic.
approaches.tradeoffs: Avoids hash map, but adds sorting overhead and index-tracking complexity.
approaches.say_it: Another option is to sort value-index pairs and use two pointers converging toward the target, but that costs an unnecessary O(n log n) sort when a single hash-map pass does it in O(n).

approaches.name: One-pass hash map
approaches.idea: Walk the array once, and for each number check if its complement (target - num) was already seen; if so, return both indices.
approaches.tradeoffs: Uses O(n) extra space for the map, but gives optimal O(n) time with simple, clean code.
approaches.say_it: I'll do a single pass with a hash map from value to index: for each number I check if its complement is already in the map, and if so I immediately have my answer — this is O(n) time and O(n) space.

blocks.name: Setup
blocks.purpose: Define function signature, no extra imports needed
blocks.code: def two_sum(nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:

blocks.name: Initialize seen map
blocks.purpose: Hash map to remember value -> index of elements already visited

blocks.name: Core loop with complement lookup
blocks.purpose: For each element, check if its complement was already seen; if so, pair found
blocks.pseudo:
for i, num in enumerate(nums):
  comp = target - num
  if comp in seen: return [seen[comp], i]
  seen[num] = i

blocks.name: Fallback return
blocks.purpose: Problem guarantees a solution exists, but keep function total for safety

steps: Go through the numbers one at a time, keeping a lookup table of every value you've already seen and its position.
For each number, work out what other number it would need to pair with to hit the target.
Check the lookup table to see if that needed number has already shown up.
If it has, you've found your pair — return the earlier position and the current position.
If it hasn't, add the current number and its position to the lookup table and move on.
Because the problem guarantees exactly one answer, you're done as soon as you find a match.
example: At 2, I need a 7 to complete the pair; I haven't seen one, so I just remember that 2 is at position 0.
At 7, I need a 2; I have seen a 2, at position 0, so I return positions 0 and 1.
That matches the expected output of [0, 1].
edge: If the array has fewer than two elements, there's no valid pair, though the problem guarantees one exists so this shouldn't come up.
Negative numbers and duplicates work the same way since the lookup table is keyed by value, not sign or uniqueness of appearance.
walkthrough.why: Storing each value's position as you scan turns the search for a matching complement into a constant-time lookup instead of a nested search, so the whole array is processed in a single linear pass.
